BRA.hook: Borders every country in South America except Chile and Ecuador — ten neighbours, more than any country outside Russia and China.
BRA.place: Fills the whole eastern bulge. If you can draw Brazil, the rest of the continent is the leftovers around it.
BRA.borders: The 1750 Treaty of Madrid swapped the paper Tordesillas line for where Portuguese settlers actually were — which is why Brazil bulges far west of the original divide; most modern edges are watershed and river lines negotiated peacefully around 1900 by the diplomat Rio Branco.

ARG.hook: Home to Aconcagua, at 6,961m the highest peak anywhere outside Asia — and it sits barely 100km from the Chilean border.
ARG.place: The long southern wedge below Brazil, sharing the Andes spine with Chile the whole way down.
ARG.borders: The 1881 treaty with Chile put the border on 'the highest peaks dividing the waters' of the Andes — a formula ambiguous enough to feed disputes for a century; the northern lines follow the Pilcomayo and Paraná rivers after wars and arbitrations.

COL.hook: The only country in South America with coastline on both the Pacific and the Caribbean.
COL.place: The top-left corner of the continent, and the only one that touches Panama — the land bridge to North America.
COL.borders: Spanish viceroyalty lines trimmed by losses: Panama seceded with US backing in 1903, and the southern Amazon reach down to Leticia survived a 1932–33 border war with Peru.

PER.hook: The Amazon starts here, in Andean meltwater, and runs the width of the continent before reaching the Atlantic in Brazil.
PER.place: Pacific coast, just south of the equator. Ecuador and Colombia above, Chile below, Brazil behind the mountains.
PER.borders: Colonial audiencia lines fought over ever since: the nitrate-rich south went to Chile in the War of the Pacific (1879–83), and the Ecuador line in the Cordillera del Cóndor was only demarcated after a 1995 war and the 1998 peace.

VEN.hook: Angel Falls drops 979m, so tall the water atomises into mist before it lands.
VEN.place: The Caribbean shoulder, east of Colombia. Trinidad sits just off its northeast tip.
VEN.borders: The old Captaincy General's limits — except in the east, where an 1899 arbitration drew the Essequibo line with British Guiana. Venezuela repudiated that award and still claims everything west of the Essequibo river.

CHL.hook: 4,300km long and averages 180km wide — the same proportions as a country stretched from Norway to the Sahara.
CHL.place: The ribbon down the Pacific edge, pinned between the Andes and the ocean for its entire length.
CHL.borders: A ribbon pinned between the Andes crest and the Pacific by the 1881 treaty with Argentina; the northern third — Bolivia's coast and Peru's Tarapacá — was won in the War of the Pacific, which is why Bolivia is landlocked.

BOL.hook: Landlocked since 1884, and still keeps a navy — it patrols Lake Titicaca and waits for the sea to come back.
BOL.place: The landlocked heart of the continent, ringed by Brazil, Peru, Chile, Argentina and Paraguay.
BOL.borders: A map of losses: the Pacific coast to Chile (1879–83), the rubber-rich Acre to Brazil (1903), and much of the Chaco to Paraguay after the bloody 1932–35 war — each defeat carved today's outline.

ECU.hook: Named after the equator, which crosses just north of Quito — the only country named for a line of latitude.
ECU.place: A small Pacific notch between Colombia and Peru. The Galápagos belong to it, 900km out to sea.
ECU.borders: Colonial Quito's claimed Amazon wedge appeared on its maps until 1998: most of it went to Peru in the 1941 war and the Rio Protocol, and the final Cordillera del Cóndor stretch was settled after the 1995 Cenepa war.

PRY.hook: Runs almost entirely on the Itaipú dam and sells the surplus to Brazil, making it one of the world's largest electricity exporters per head.
PRY.place: The other landlocked one, tucked between Bolivia, Brazil and Argentina.
PRY.borders: Rivers nearly all the way round — Paraná, Paraguay, Pilcomayo. It lost swathes of territory after the catastrophic War of the Triple Alliance (1864–70), then won most of the disputed Chaco from Bolivia in the 1930s.

URY.hook: Smaller than every other Spanish-speaking country in South America, with more cattle than people — about four to one.
URY.place: The small wedge on the Atlantic between Brazil and Argentina, across the river from Buenos Aires.
URY.borders: Created whole as a buffer state: Britain brokered its independence in 1828 precisely so neither Brazil nor Argentina would hold both banks of the Río de la Plata; the Uruguay river draws the western line.

GUY.hook: The only country in South America where English is the official language — and since a 2015 offshore oil strike, among the fastest-growing economies on Earth.
GUY.place: One of the three small countries stacked along the northeast coast, east of Venezuela.
GUY.borders: British Guiana's colonial limits: the west is the 1899 arbitration line Venezuela still rejects (it claims all land west of the Essequibo), and the southeastern New River triangle is likewise claimed by Suriname.

SUR.hook: Dutch-speaking, and the smallest sovereign country in South America — most of it is rainforest almost nobody lives in.
SUR.place: The middle of the three northeastern neighbours: Guyana to its west, French Guiana to its east.
SUR.borders: Dutch Guiana's edges are two rivers — the Corentyne west, the Maroni east — but each has rival headstreams upstream, so both ends of the country are still quietly disputed with its neighbours.
